lines.text: This is your 10-minute Walk Edition of My Six-Year-Old Can't Do Five Things at Once, So His Screen Shows One. Start walking. I'll tell you when you're halfway.
lines.speaker: app

lines.text: My son is six and started kindergarten a month ago.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A school morning asks him for five things: eat, brush teeth, get dressed, shoes and jacket, backpack.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Breakfast is easy, because breakfast is one pancake with honey and he is very consistent about that.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The rest is where it falls apart.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: He starts getting dressed, remembers his teeth, wants to play, and a few minutes later he is doing all three at once, which means none of them.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I noticed that he is fine with any single step.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What he cannot hold is the list.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: So I built a screen for him that never shows a list.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: One Thing is a small app for our home network.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I type the routine in plain words.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A Gemma 4 model running on my laptop turns it into a short mission with a theme (I went with rockets).
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I read every step and fix what I don't like.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Only after I approve it does it reach the kid screen on the tablet, and there it shows exactly one step at a time: one big emoji, a few words, and one button.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Every rule on that screen comes from something I see on our mornings:
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: One step on screen, never a list.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Every step is read aloud.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The button has to be held, not tapped.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Brushing teeth is a timer he can't skip.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Nothing ever fails.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The end is always visible.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I approve every mission first.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Try the kid screen yourself: nazboyko.github.io/one-thing/demo.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It plays the built-in sample mission in your browser.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Hold the amber button; a quick tap does nothing.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: In the video (79 seconds) I type a routine for getting ready to go outside and give it the theme "space walk".
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Gemma writes the mission in 2.6 seconds.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I scroll through the steps, approve it, and the kid screen plays the mission to the finale.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The typing is sped up 2x and labeled.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The kid screen runs at normal speed, and you can hear it say each step.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: This is the first working version.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I built it in one evening.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: My son has not used it yet.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I wanted it finished and checked before it goes in front of him.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The open-source AI at the center is Gemma 4, Google's open-weight model (gemma4:e4b, with thinking turned off).
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Ollama, an open-source runtime, runs it on my laptop.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Around them sits one Go binary that uses only the standard library, with a React front end compiled into it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There is no database, no account and no cloud.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Saved missions are JSON files in a folder, and the only network call the app makes is to Ollama on localhost.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The Go server sends JSON to Ollama running Gemma 4 on the laptop.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The server sanitizes, validates, and retries the JSON.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The parent reads, edits, and approves the mission.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The tablet then shows one step at a time.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Getting a small model to return something I can trust.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I don't want prose from the model.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I want a mission my code can check.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: So the request to Ollama carries a JSON schema, and Gemma has to answer in that shape.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A mission holds three to eight steps, and each step is described like this:
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The code defines an object structure.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: This structure requires an emoji, title, say, mode, and seconds.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The mode can be until_done or for_duration.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A schema guarantees the shape, not the sense.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: So every answer goes through two more functions.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Sanitize fixes what is safe to fix: stray whitespace, Title Case in step titles, a timer outside the allowed range, an "emoji" that is not one.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Validate returns plain field errors such as steps[2].title: too many words (at most 6).
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If any remain, the server sends them back to the model as a follow-up message and asks once more.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Here is what I typed:
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Routine: School morning for a 6-year-old: breakfast, brush teeth, get dressed, shoes and jacket, backpack.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Brushing teeth is the hardest part, split it into short pieces.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Theme: rocket launch
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: And this is the raw answer, with only the line breaks tidied:
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The code shows a rocket launch preparation sequence.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It includes steps like fueling up, polishing teeth, suiting up, sealing gear, and packing the rocket.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I would still change one line before approving it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: "Keep fueling up!" sounds like "eat more", which the prompt tells the model never to say.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Numbers from my laptop (Apple M5 Max, 64 GB, Ollama 0.35, model already loaded):
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Thinking off averaged 2.4 seconds per mission, and it was valid on the first try for 22 of 22 runs.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Thinking on took 11.3 seconds for one run and was not valid.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: You're halfway. If you're walking out and back, turn around now.
lines.speaker: app

lines.text: The 22 runs went through the server while I tuned the prompt (school mornings, a bedtime, an after-school routine), and the time includes parsing and validation.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The retry never fired; it is covered by tests against a fake Ollama.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Thinking made Gemma several times slower and worse at this job, so it stays off.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The prompt needed real fixes.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The first version returned valid JSON every time, and as a parent I would still have rejected half of it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Asked for "breakfast", it invented cereal.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Asked to split tooth brushing because it is the hardest part, a bedtime run kept it as one two-minute step.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: So the prompt now says:
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The code ensures only named actions are used.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It also forces hard parts to become two or three separate steps.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Brushing has been split in every run since.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Two more fixes came from reading output the same way: one run said "eat your breakfast until done", and another made breakfast a two-minute timed step, which would have locked the button while he eats.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What did not work.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: In 3 of 8 morning runs that I read line by line, Gemma folded "shoes and jacket" into just "shoes".
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Four rounds of prompt changes fixed everything else I found, but not this.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The screenshot shows it happening again, unedited: step 5 has no jacket.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: This is why the parent reads every step before approving, and why I would not let a model talk to my son directly.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Small things that turned out to matter:
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The hold button fires after 0.8 seconds, measured from timestamps, not animation frames.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Quick taps do nothing, and letting go early drains the ring.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Step timers come from timestamps too, so a throttled tab stays correct.?speed=20 in the address makes them twenty times faster, which is how the screen got tested without brushing anyone's teeth for a minute at a time.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Gemma once returned a colon as the "emoji" for both teeth steps, and my validator let it through: it only rejected letters and digits.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Now any plain ASCII there is rejected and replaced with a star.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The first voice the app picked sounded robotic.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It now uses only voices installed on the device, never a network one: Premium first, then Enhanced, then a short list of natural voices, and never the novelty voices macOS ships.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: On the parent screen I can pick another voice and test it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If I set a time to leave, the last screen says how long is left: "You have 14 minutes to play before liftoff."
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What I cut.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A speed comparison with the smaller gemma4:e2b.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It was not on the laptop, so I have no numbers for it.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It was one evening, and the kid screen got the time.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: What is not tested yet.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It has run in a browser in tablet mode on my laptop, not on a real tablet, and not with the person it is for.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Speech voices differ between devices: for a natural one on a Mac or iPad, you download a Premium or Enhanced English voice in Settings > Accessibility > Spoken Content (Read & Speak on newer macOS), and the app picks it by itself.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I expect the timers to need tuning once a real six-year-old is holding the button.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: For this project it is not a nice extra.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It decides whether I would use the thing at all.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The input is a description of where my child struggles.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: "Brushing teeth is the hardest part."
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: "He only eats one thing for breakfast."
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: That is what I type into the box.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: With open weights on my own laptop, those sentences go from my keyboard to my own memory and nowhere else.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I did not have to read anyone's privacy policy to decide that this was fine.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It does not need the internet.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The page, the Lexend font, the model and the saved missions all live on the laptop.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: A morning routine should not depend on somebody else's uptime.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: It costs nothing, so I can be picky.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: I generated dozens of missions while tuning the prompt.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: There is no meter running, no key to protect, and no account to create for a tool that a six-year-old uses.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Anyone can change how it thinks.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The system prompt is a text file in the repository.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: The model is one line of configuration.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: If your kid needs steps cut even smaller, you edit a paragraph of English.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: For a family tool, local and open is simply the right shape.
lines.speaker: source

lines.text: Here is something to think about on the way back. Considering the system's reliance on a parent to approve every step, what does that reveal about the necessary level of human oversight when customizing a tool for a child's specific needs?
lines.speaker: app

lines.text: That's the end. You should be almost home.
lines.speaker: app
